intro: Eight questions, two per track, about a minute each. Answer what you know and choose **Not sure** for the rest. The guide suggests the first track where a question gets past you. Nothing is graded and you can retake it.

questions.q: You edit a file and run `git commit -m "Update"`. Git answers that there is nothing to commit. What is the usual reason?
choices: The change was never staged with `git add`
You have to push before you can commit
The commit message is too short
The file is too large for Git
questions.why: A commit records what is in the staging area, not what is in your working tree. Until you stage the change with `git add`, or use `git commit -a` for tracked files, the commit has nothing to record.

choices: Uploads your commits to GitHub
Opens a pull request
Downloads new commits and merges them into your current branch
Throws away your local changes
questions.why: Pull is fetch followed by merge. It downloads what the remote has and integrates it into the branch you are on. A pull request is a GitHub feature with a similar name and a different job.

questions.q: Two people change different lines, far apart, in the same file on different branches. What happens when the branches merge?
choices: A conflict, because the same file changed twice
Git combines both changes on its own
The later commit replaces the earlier one
Git asks which whole file to keep
questions.why: Git merges regions of lines, not whole files. A conflict needs both sides to change the same or adjacent lines in different ways.

questions.q: You pushed a commit that broke something, and teammates have already pulled it. Which undo is safe?
choices: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, then force-push
`git commit --amend`, then push
Delete the branch on GitHub and push it again
`git revert` the commit, then push
questions.why: Revert adds a new commit that applies the opposite change, so everyone's history stays valid. Reset and amend rewrite history other people already have, which forces them to repair their clones.

questions.q: In a GitHub Actions workflow, how do jobs and steps relate?
choices: A job is a list of steps that run in order on one runner
A step contains several jobs
They are two names for the same thing
Steps run in parallel and jobs run in order
questions.why: A workflow has jobs. Each job gets a fresh runner and executes its steps in order. Jobs run in parallel unless one declares that it needs another.

questions.q: After a rebase you must overwrite a branch you already pushed. Which push will refuse if a teammate pushed commits you have not seen?
choices: `git push --force`
`git push --all`
`git push --force-with-lease`
`git push -u origin HEAD`
questions.why: `--force-with-lease` overwrites only if the remote branch is still where your last fetch saw it. Plain `--force` overwrites whatever is there, including work you never saw.

questions.q: You change the message of a commit from three commits back. Why do the ids of the later commits change too?
choices: Git renumbers commits so they stay in order
GitHub issues new ids when you push
Each commit's id is a hash that covers its parent's id
The timestamps are refreshed
questions.why: A commit's id is a hash of its content, and that content includes the id of its parent. Change one commit and every descendant must be rewritten with a new id. That chain is what makes history tamper-evident.

questions.q: A workflow step runs `echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"` inside a `run:` script. What is the risk?
choices: None. GitHub sanitizes titles before the workflow sees them
Script injection: the title is pasted into the script before the shell runs it
The title will be masked as a secret in the log
The step only fails on pull requests from forks
questions.why: The expression is replaced with the raw title before the shell starts, so a title containing shell syntax runs as code. Pass untrusted values through an environment variable and quote the variable instead.
